interactive.title: Equal steps on a power ladder
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens on the power ladder. Its rungs are the powers of one base, drawn equally spaced up the screen with each rung's value beside it. For base 8 they are 8⁰ = 1, 8¹ = 8, 8² = 64 and 8³ = 512, so each step up puts one more 8 into the multiplying, as in lesson 1, and multiplies by 8. The height on the ladder is the power, and the number beside it is the value. On the first screen, with the ladder already drawn, three buttons cut every step into 2, 3 or 4 equal small steps, opening at 3, and a stepper climbs one small step at a time. Each small step adds the same fraction to the power, and adding to a power multiplies the value, as lesson 1's adding law says, so every small step multiplies by the same number whichever rung it starts from. Three small steps must make one step of × 8, so each is × 2, because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, and the first small step lands on 8^(1/3) = 2. Cut into 2, each small step is × √8, about 2.83, and cut into 4 it is about × 1.68: roots that are not whole, written to two places. Screen 3 uses base 4 cut into halves: two small steps of × 2 make one step of × 4, so 4^(1/2) = √4 = 2. Screen 5 climbs two small steps on the base-8 ladder: × 2 then × 2 lands on 4, which is 8^(2/3). Screen 7 has a Root first / Power first switch for 27^(5/3) on a base-27 ladder. Root first cuts each step into three small steps of × 3 and climbs five of them, to 3⁵ = 243. Power first climbs five whole steps, to 27⁵ = 14,348,907, then takes the cube root, which keeps a third of that height, and lands on the same rung, 243. Both are 27^(5/3), because a power of a power multiplies the powers: ⅓ × 5 and 5 × ⅓ are the same. Screen 9 carries the base-8 ladder below 1: each small step down divides by 2, so two small steps down land on 1/4, which is 8^(−2/3), and the ladder gets smaller without reaching nothing. Screen 11 multiplies on the base-4 ladder: half a step, × 2, then three half steps, × 8, make four half steps, two whole steps, so 4^(1/2) × 4^(3/2) = 2 × 8 = 16 = 4². Screen 13 finds a cube tank's edge on the base-8 ladder carried below 1: 0.125 is the rung 8⁻¹, one whole step down, and its cube root is a third of that height, one small step down, 8^(−1/3) = 0.5. Screen 14 takes 16^(−3/4) three small steps of ÷ 2 down the base-16 ladder, to 1/8. Screens 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 show an idea, screens 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 ask you to try it, and screens 13 and 14 mix them. A puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick climbs its own small steps beside the right ones, so you can see where it lands: three small steps of × 9 reach 729, not 27.
interactive.ignores: The rungs are drawn equally spaced although each value is 8 times the last, because the height shows the power, not the size of the number; drawn to size, 512 would be off the screen. Roots that are not whole are rounded on screen, mostly to two places, and the root itself is exact. The slider cuts a step into 2, 3 or 4, but any whole number of equal small steps works the same way, and a power such as 1.3 sits between the rungs too. Only positive bases are drawn, and everything the lesson says is about positive numbers. A negative base needs more care: (−8)^(1/3) is usually taken as the real cube root, −2, but (−4)^(1/2) has no answer among ordinary numbers. A positive number has two square roots, 2 and −2 for 4, as lesson 3 showed, and 4^(1/2), like √4, means the positive one. The puzzles' numbers are examples.

explain.text:
A power that is a fraction is a root, for any positive number. The bottom number of the fraction says which root to take and the top number says what power to raise it to, so 8^(1/3) is the cube root of 8, which is 2, and 27^(5/3) is the cube root of 27, which is 3, raised to the power 5, which is 243.

Start from lesson 1's adding law. On the power ladder, rungs 1, 8, 64 and 512 are 8⁰, 8¹, 8² and 8³, and each step up multiplies by 8. Now cut one step into three equal small steps, each adding ⅓ to the power. Adding ⅓ to a power multiplies by 8^(1/3), whichever rung you start from, so every small step multiplies by the same number. Three of them make one whole step, because multiplying adds the powers and ⅓ + ⅓ + ⅓ = 1, so 8^(1/3) × 8^(1/3) × 8^(1/3) = 8¹ = 8.[^1] So 8^(1/3) is the number that, used three times in a multiplication, makes 8. That is 2, because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, so 8^(1/3) = ∛8 = 2, the cube root of lesson 3. The power-of-a-power law agrees: (8^(1/3))³ = 8^(⅓ × 3) = 8¹, which is why a fraction as a power is defined as a root.[^2][^3] Cut a step into two instead and 4^(1/2) × 4^(1/2) = 4¹, so 4^(1/2) = √4 = 2. Cut it into four and you get the [[fourth root]]: 16^(1/4) = 2, because 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. The bottom of the fraction counts the equal small steps in one whole step, so it is the root.

The top number counts the small steps you climb. 8^(2/3) is two small steps of × 2, so 8^(2/3) = (∛8)² = 4. A power like this is a [[fractional power]]: the numerator tells you the power and the denominator tells you the root.[^4] 27^(5/3) is five small steps of × 3, so it is 3⁵ = 243. You can take the power first instead: 27⁵ = 14,348,907, and its cube root is 243 as well. Both ways are the power-of-a-power law, (27^(1/3))⁵ = 27^(⅓ × 5) and (27⁵)^(1/3) = 27^(5 × ⅓), and ⅓ × 5 = 5 × ⅓.[^2] Root first usually keeps the numbers small. A minus still means one over, as in lesson 2: 8^(−2/3) = 1/8^(2/3) = 1/4, a small amount, not a negative one.[^5] And multiplying still adds the powers: x^(1/2) × x^(3/2) = x^(1/2 + 3/2) = x². Two slips are worth seeing fail. 8^(1/3) is not 8 × ⅓ ≈ 2.67, because three steps of × 2.67 come to about 19, not 8. And the root goes on the bottom: 64^(2/3) = (∛64)² = 16, while (√64)³ = 512 is 64^(3/2). Square roots of negative numbers, and powers that can be any number, wait for Complex numbers and Exponentials and logarithms.

**A fractional power is a root: the bottom number of the fraction is the root and the top number is the power, so 8^(1/3) = 2 and 27^(5/3) = 3⁵ = 243.[^3][^4]**

analogy.text: Say a gearbox brings 8 turns of the motor down to 1 turn of the shaft in three stages that are all the same, and you want each stage's ratio. Stages in a row multiply: two 2:1 stages make 4:1, and three make 8:1. So each stage is 2:1, the cube root of 8. Finding the stage from the total is what a fractional power does: three small steps of × 2 make one step of × 8 on the ladder.
analogy.breaks: A real stage's ratio is set by whole numbers of teeth, so splitting 10:1 into three equal stages, about 2.15:1 each, can only be got close to. A number has no such limit: 10^(1/3) is exact, written as ∛10.

practice.text:
- Read the fraction: the bottom number is the root, the top number is the power.
- Take the root first, because it usually keeps the numbers small: for 27^(5/3), ∛27 = 3.
- Check the root by multiplying it back: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.
- Then raise it to the power: 3⁵ = 243.
- A minus in the power means one over: put the answer under 1.
- Multiplying powers of the same base, add the fractions; raising a power to a power, multiply them.

**Rule of thumb:** A power of ½ is a square root and a power of ⅓ is a cube root.

**On a calculator** (not from this lesson's sources): on a one-line display, put the power in brackets, 27 ^ ( 5 ÷ 3 ), which gives 243. Without them the calculator can work out 27⁵ ÷ 3 = 4,782,969 instead. On a calculator that shows a raised box for the power, type the whole fraction inside the box. A decimal power such as 1.3 is a fraction too: 2^1.3 is 2^(13/10), between 2¹ = 2 and 2² = 4, and a calculator gives about 2.46.

**Worked example:** A cube-shaped tank holds 0.343 m³. Its edge, used three times in a multiplication, makes the volume, so the edge is 0.343^(1/3) = ∛0.343 = 0.7 m. Check: 0.7 × 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.343. A harder one, 16^(−3/4): the bottom number is 4, so take the fourth root, 2, because 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. The top number is 3, so cube it: 2³ = 8. The minus means one over, so 16^(−3/4) = 1/8 = 0.125. Power first gives the same: 16³ = 4096, its fourth root is 8, and one over that is 1/8.

**Common mistakes**
- Multiplying by the fraction: 8^(1/3) is 2, not 8 × ⅓ ≈ 2.67.
- Adding the fraction: 49^(1/2) is 7, not 49 + ½ = 49.5.
- The root on top: 64^(2/3) is (∛64)² = 16, not (√64)³ = 512.
- Reading the minus as a negative answer, a common slip with negative powers:[^6] 27^(−1/3) is 1/3, not −3.
- Multiplying the powers when you multiply: x^(1/2) × x^(3/2) is x², not x^(3/4).

interactive.html:
A power ladder: each rung is a power of one base, drawn equally spaced up the page with its value beside it. The bases and numbers tried are examples.

Each small step adds the same fraction to the power, so every small step multiplies by the same number.
interactive.title: Equal steps on a power ladder
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is three equal small steps of × 2 landing exactly on the next rung, 8, so 8^(1/3) = 2, when you climb the power ladder one small step at a time.

checks.label: The base numbers are the same, so add the indices together (9³ × 9⁵ = 9⁸): on the 8 ladder every small step adds the same fraction to the power, so at each cut, 2, 3 or 4, every rung climbed from 1 to 512 is the one below it times the same number

Fractional exponents are defined as roots, from the rule for powers of powers: at each cut c on the first screen, one small step used c times in a multiplication makes the whole step of × 8, and at cut 3 each small step is × 2, so 8^(1/3) = ∛8 = 2

The numerator tells us the power and the denominator tells us the root: in each puzzle that asks for a fractional power, the ladder cuts every step into the bottom number of small steps, the right climb takes the top number of them, and it stops on the root raised to that power

To raise to a power for a given base, multiply the indices: on the 27 ladder, root first (five small steps of × 3) and power first (five whole steps of × 27 to 14,348,907, then a third of that height) both stop on 27^(5/3) = 243

To raise to a power for a given base, multiply the indices: on the tank screen 0.125 is the rung 8⁻¹, one whole step below 1, and the right climb stops a third of that height down, on 8^(−1/3) = 0.5, where 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125

A negative power gives the reciprocal of the number, 1 over the number: two small steps down the 8 ladder land on 8^(−2/3) = 1/4, one over 8^(2/3) = 4, and one small step down the 27 ladder on 27^(−1/3) = 1/3, one over ∛27

A common misconception is that since the power is negative, the result must be negative, and this is not so: every rung on every ladder in the lesson, those below 1 included, holds a positive amount, and the picks −3 and −9 are drawn below 0, off the ladder
Every line of working on every screen adds up, the first screen's at each cut, 2, 3 and 4

Each puzzle accepts only its right answer, which equals the question, and the right climb stops on the rung of that value; before an answer no small rung shows a value; each wrong pick draws its own steps or mark on the ladder where its number sits, or below 0 off it
The rungs are equally spaced: on every ladder each small step is the same height, and the value beside each rung is the one below it times the same number
Every demonstration has arrived within 5 s of its screen opening, nothing before the 0.35 s screen fade; every answer's motion, and every move on the first screen, within 3 s
